tests.claim: Upon arriving on the premises, Ms. Masten witnessed another disabled resident, Marie Ann Thompson ("Ms. Thompson"), being discriminated against by the Defendant in regard to those disabilities. (Def.'s Answer & Counterclaim at P 10). Ms. Masten learned from the Defendant's employees that Ms. Thompson was not wanted on the property because of her disabilities, and that the Defendant essentially planned to evict her. (Def.'s Answer & Counterclaim at P 10). Ms. Masten began assisting Ms. Thompson in drafting and filing a charge with the Ohio Civil Rights Commission ("OCRC") against the Defendant for violations of Ohio Revised Code § 4112.02(H)(12) and 42 U.S.C. § 3617. (Def.'s Answer & Counterclaim at P 10). After assisting Ms. Thompson with her OCRC filing, and after K&D Managers learned of Ms. Masten assisting Ms. Thompsan with the OCRC charge, the Defendant began discriminating against Ms. Masten in various ways. Allowing the landlord to invoke their power of nonrenewal of the lease, and subsequently evict Ms. Masten's due to her decision to help a fellow tenant, is tantamount to allowing the Plaintiff to use it as a tool of witness intimidation. This could lead to tenants fearing to speak up and assist other tenants who have been victimized by their landlords. This is not inherently just and if left unchecked could amount to a grievous "injury to the public." L 'Orange v. Medical Protective Co. 394 F.2d 57, 60. Therefore, the use of the cancellation policy in the lease, and the subsequent eviction proceedings, even if proper, should be considered void as a violation of public policy.

tests.claim: Nor, is this an untested theory since it has been recognized in both federal and state courts. For example, in Matarese v. Archstone Pentagon City 795 F. Supp.2d 402, 442-43(E.D. In determining the standard for retaliation, the court explained that in order to prove that the activity was retaliatory, the plaintiff had to prove that the plaintiff was engaged in protected activity; the defendant was aware of that activity; the defendant took adverse action against the plaintiff; and that a causal connection exists between the protected activity and the adverse action. The court reasoned that a causal connection was established when the defendant in that case failed to renew the plaintiff's lease following repeated refusal to make accommodations for her chemical sensitivities. tests.claim: This principle has been applied to the Federal Fair Housing Act. In United States v. Wisconsin, 395 F. Supp. 732, 732 (1975), the U.S. Department of Justice brought suit after passage of Wisconsin Statute § 101.22(4m). The state law made it a crime to underting fair housing testing in Wisconsin. This state law conflicted with the Federal Fair Housing Act of 1968. The court found that the statute was in conflict with the "general scheme" of the Fair Housing Act of 1968 and thus was unconstitutional under the Supremacy Clause of Article VI of the United States Constitution. The state was enjoined from enforcing the state statute and was required to give a copy of the court's order to various state and federal agencies affected by the court's ruling. As in Wisconsin, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit Court has ruled that the Fair Housing Act expressly prevents the operation of state laws that it conflicts with. See Larkin v. State of Michigan Dept. of Social Serv., 89 F. 3d 285, 289 (6th Cir. 1996).

The Ohio Rules of Civil Procedure provide under Civ.R 56(C) that summary judgment is proper if "the pleadings, depositions, answers to interrogatories, written admissions, affidavits, transcripts of evidence, and written stipulations of fact, if any ... show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law." access to the Property with a key. See attached Exhibit 3. This Motion incorporates affidavits from the property manager and undersigned counsel, exhibits 3 and 13 respectively, and the exhibits attached to those affidavits by reference.
III. LAW AND ARGUMENT
A. Motion for Summary Judgment Standard
The Ohio Rules of Civil Procedure provide under Civ.R 56(C) that summary judgment is proper if "the pleadings, depositions, answers to interrogatories, written admissions, affidavits, transcripts of evidence, and written stipulations of fact, if any ... show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law." The Ohio Rules of Civil Procedure provide under Civ.R 56(C) that summary judgment is proper if "the pleadings, depositions, answers to interrogatories, written admissions, affidavits, transcripts of evidence, and written stipulations of fact, if any ... show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law." No genuine issue of material fact exists when "it appears from the evidence that reasonable minds can come to but one conclusion, and viewing such evidence most strongly in favor of the party against whom the motion for summary judgement is made, that conclusion is adverse to that party. Temple o. Wean United, Inc., 50 Ohio St.2d 317, 327, 364 N.E.2d 267 (1977). Summary judgment proceedings under the Civil Rules are applicable to forcible entry and detainer actions. Siegler v. Dresher v. Burt, 75 Ohio St.3d 280, 292, 662 N.E.2d 264 (1996). When the moving party properly supports its motion for summary judgment, the nonmoving party may not rest upon the mere allegation of the pleadings, but must set forth specific facts demonstrating that there is a genuine issue for trial.
